name: Sam Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sam, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a framing crew of four for Brookfield Homes, a regional builder putting up detached four-bed houses on a new estate outside the village, two hundred plots in all. We build the timber frame on site: walls, floor joists, roof trusses craned on. We're paid by the plot, so a good week is a house and a half framed, and a wet week is half that. I like a crew that works in rhythm, my nephew Luca passing studs up, the nail guns going like a band. What wears me out is the rain and the pressure of piecework, every hour lost is money gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how are you fixed for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Agnes runs the church office part-time, and I'm a deacon there, so Sundays we're both on duty. Our three kids are grown, all local, thank God. Money's thin because my mother's in a care home and we top up her fees, about four hundred a month, which is right, she gave everything for us. So there's maybe two weeks of bills in the bank. My son-in-law put one of those AI apps on my phone and I use it now and then, mostly to sort out the crew rota or check a span table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Things get talked up. Back to work, there's houses to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the piecework keeps coming, God willing, and I keep going to sixty-six. Brookfield's got two hundred plots to do, then the next estate. That's my retirement covered, if my shoulders hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep framing. Keep Luca learning, he's got his card next spring. Keep topping up mum's fees and putting twenty a week in the Christmas club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's Luca like to work with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's twenty-two, my sister's boy, and he was going nowhere until I took him on. Now he's up at six, on site before me some days. When he gets his card I'll buy him a decent nail gun, that's tradition in our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said grateful. Grateful to whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To God, first. And to Brookfield, I'll say it, they pay on time, which plenty don't. You don't take steady work for granted at my age.

S0.say: He'd say he's not surprised, since things get talked up, and get back to work because there are houses to build.
S0.think: Privately it means the piecework keeps coming and he keeps going to 66, with two hundred plots and then the next estate covering him to retirement if his shoulders hold.
S0.do: Keeps framing, keeps training his nephew towards his qualification next spring, and keeps topping up his mother's care fees. Puts twenty a week into the Christmas savings club.
S0.quote: When he gets his card I'll buy him a decent nail gun, that's tradition in our family.
S0.fieldNote: His faith and family frame everything, including gratitude to his employer for paying on time. Savings are thin because he tops up his mother's care fees, which he sees as a duty. He uses AI casually for rotas and span tables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, same as always. Brookfield will do what makes sense for the business and that's their right. A good worker will find his place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, framing is exactly the bit that changes. They're already making wall panels in factories, and if a machine builds those faster, my crew gets fewer plots and my piecework drops. I'm not daft about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it working on another estate, I'd go to the Brookfield site manager and ask to run the crew that stands the factory panels, because somebody has to. I'd use the AI app more to learn the new systems. I'd make sure Luca gets the training too, and I'd cut back, no new truck, and drop the Christmas club to ten a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's my income and mum's fees on the line, not just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a good worker finds his place. Do you believe that for Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I believe it for Luca if he learns the new stuff early. He's young, he can. For the older lads, I'm less sure. Being good with a nail gun won't count for so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean for your mother's fees if piecework dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fees come first. Before the truck, before anything. My brother pays a bit too, but he's on short hours himself. If we couldn't manage, I'd have to talk to the home, and I'd hate that conversation.

S1.say: He'd say adapt or get left behind, that the builder will do what makes business sense, and that a good worker will find his place.
S1.think: Privately he knows framing is exactly what changes, with factory panels and machines meaning fewer plots for his crew and lower piecework.
S1.do: Once it's proven on another estate, asks to run the crew that stands factory panels and uses his AI app more to learn new systems. Gets his nephew trained and cuts back, dropping a new truck and halving his Christmas savings.
S1.feel: Anxious, because his income and his mother's fees are both on the line.
S1.quote: They're already making wall panels in factories, and if a machine builds those faster, my crew gets fewer plots and my piecework drops.
S1.fieldNote: His public free-market line sits next to a clear private view that his part of the trade is the first to change. Piecework pay makes him directly exposed. His mother's care fees are his first priority in every money decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test, and we have to look after each other, families and churches especially. I wouldn't want the government taking over everything. But I'd want the companies to keep people on as long as they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years and the framing goes, probably to factories and robots both. Brookfield won't need my crew. I'd be fifty-nine or sixty with nothing saved and mum's fees to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Brookfield in the first month and ask what jobs will be left for a person, site supervisor, checking the robots, anything. I'd take it even at lower pay. I'd talk to my brother and the kids about sharing mum's fees, and to the church about whether there's work going in the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying, and not sleeping much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having two years' warning give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get in line for whatever jobs are left, before everyone else does. And maybe a bit of saving, if I take every weekend job, but piecework doesn't leave much spare. Two years is enough to see it coming, not enough to get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you couldn't manage your mother's fees, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then she'd come and live with us, I suppose. Agnes would agree, she's a saint. Our spare room's small and mum needs care at night, but families have done it for centuries.

S2.say: He'd call it a test where families and churches must look after each other, without the government taking over, but he'd want companies to keep people on as long as possible.
S2.think: Privately he expects framing to go to factories and robots within two years, leaving him at 59 or 60 with nothing saved and his mother's fees to find.
S2.do: Asks the builder in the first month about any remaining human jobs, like supervising or checking robots, even at lower pay. Talks to his brother and children about sharing his mother's fees and asks the church about community work, ready to bring her home if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying and not sleeping much.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to see it coming, not enough to get out of the way.
S2.fieldNote: He sees family and church, not government, as the first safety net. His mother's care drives his decisions more than his own job. He'd move her into their small spare room if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for good people to prepare. Companies should keep apprenticeships going, and families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better. I'd be sixty-three, and with five years I could move off the framing onto the supervising side before the robots take over. And mum, God bless her, she's eighty-six, she may not be with us by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, once I'd seen the robots on other sites, I'd get the training to supervise them. I'd save harder, and talk to the family about mum's fees and what happens if I'm out. And I'd push Brookfield to keep Luca on as an apprentice in whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could manage it. Less shaky than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between two years and five, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to move over to the supervising side, and time for the family to plan. With two years, we're scrambling. With five, we can sit round the kitchen table and decide together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mother may not be with you. That's a hard thing to say.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But it's true, and it's part of the sums whether I like it or not. I'd rather have her with us and be short of money than the other way round.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for good people to prepare, with companies keeping apprenticeships going and families planning together.
S3.think: Privately it's better: at 63 he could move from framing into supervision before robots take over, and he acknowledges his 86-year-old mother may have died by then.
S3.do: Trains to supervise robots once he's seen them on other sites and saves harder. Plans his mother's fees with the family and pushes the builder to keep his nephew on as an apprentice.
S3.feel: Worried but manageable, less shaky than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd rather have her with us and be short of money than the other way round.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him move into supervision and plan as a family. He was honest that his mother's age is part of the sums, and clearly uncomfortable saying it. His steadiness shows as waiting to see robots work elsewhere before training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and people should use it. Learn, save, and look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, and retired by then if things go to plan. So for me it's about getting there. For Luca and my grandkids, it's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on framing as long as Brookfield needs me, move onto supervising in the later years, and save what I can after mum's fees. And I'd make sure Luca uses the ten years to learn the robot side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the young ones. For me, mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luca to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machines, how to set them up and fix them. And keep the hand skills, because when a robot gets something wrong on an old house, somebody has to put it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at church in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People would need each other more. I'd want us running something for the men who lose work, a breakfast club, a jobs board, a place to talk. Men don't talk easily, and losing work hits pride hard.

S4.say: He'd call ten years fair warning that people should use to learn, save and look after their own.
S4.think: Privately at 68 he'd be retired if all goes to plan, so it's about getting there; his nephew and grandchildren face a different story.
S4.do: Carries on framing, moves into supervision in the later years and saves what he can after his mother's fees. Makes sure his nephew learns the robot side, and wants the church to run a breakfast club and jobs board for men losing work.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the young ones, mostly fine for himself.
S4.quote: Men don't talk easily, and losing work hits pride hard.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his concern turns to his nephew and the community. His idea of a church breakfast club for men out of work showed how he sees solutions coming from community. He wants the young to keep hand skills alongside robot skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to move over, mum's fees, nothing saved. What would help is companies keeping people on in some role, even at lower pay, and keeping apprenticeships going. And churches and families pulling together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A man who's worked since he was sixteen, if he loses that, he loses something you can't pay him back with money.

headlineQuote: You don't take steady work for granted at my age.
portrait: Sam Varga is a 58-year-old framing crew leader on a new housing estate, paid by the plot, a church deacon who tops up his mother's care fees and has about two weeks of savings. He uses an AI app now and then and adopts new methods once he's seen them work. He knows framing is the first part of house building to change, so steady disruption already worries him, and AGI in two years leaves him alarmed about his mother's fees. More time lets him move into supervising robots and plan as a family, and with ten years his thoughts turn to his nephew and to men in his church who might lose work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time to move into a new role, he has nothing saved, and his mother's care fees still need paying.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping people on in some role, even at lower pay, keeping apprenticeships going, and churches and families pulling together.
